subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 5.5 Rotational Equilibrium and Newton’s First Law in Rotational Form
5.6 Newton’s Second Law in Rotational Form

questions.q: A bicycle wheel turns through 1.5 revolutions about its axle. What is the magnitude of the wheel's angular displacement?
options: 1.5 rad
540 rad
3.1 rad
9.4 rad
optionWhy: A student who uses the number of revolutions as the number of radians picks this. A radian is much smaller than a revolution: one revolution is 2π ≈ 6.28 rad, so 1.5 revolutions is about 9.4 rad.
A student who works out the angle in degrees, 1.5 × 360° = 540°, and then writes the number with the unit rad picks this. 540° is 540 × (π/180) = 3π rad ≈ 9.4 rad.

A student who ignores the complete revolution, because the wheel is back in its starting orientation after it, and counts only the half turn left over (π rad) picks this. Every turn in the same sense adds 2π rad to the angular displacement.
One revolution is 2π rad, so 1.5 revolutions is 1.5 × 2π = 3π rad ≈ 9.4 rad.
questions.explain: One revolution is 2π rad, so 1.5 revolutions is 1.5 × 2π = 3π rad ≈ 9.4 rad.
questions.working: One revolution = 2π rad. Δθ = 1.5 × 2π rad = 3π rad = 9.42 rad ≈ 9.4 rad.

questions.q: A bicycle is held upside down, and one of its wheels is set spinning about its axle, which stays fixed. Which statement correctly describes the motion of points on the spinning wheel?
options: Every point on the wheel moves in the same direction, since the wheel keeps its shape.
Points at the top and at the bottom of the wheel move in opposite directions.
No point on the wheel moves, since the wheel's center of mass stays at rest.
Points near the rim turn through larger angles than points near the axle.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a system that keeps its shape must move as one piece picks this. That is true of a block sliding without rotating, but in rotation each point follows its own circle, so points on opposite sides of the axle move in opposite directions.

The wheel is a rigid system: it holds its shape, but each point moves around its own circle about the axle. At any instant the top of the rim moves one way and the bottom moves the opposite way, which is why the spinning wheel cannot be modeled as an object with a single velocity.

A student who judges whether a system moves only from its center of mass picks this. The center of mass does stay at the axle, but every other point of the wheel moves in a circle about it; the rotation is described with angular quantities.

A student who expects points farther out to rotate more picks this. Points near the rim travel farther, along larger circles, but every line drawn from the axle sweeps the same angle in the same time, so all points turn through the same angle.
questions.explain: The wheel is a rigid system: it holds its shape, but each point moves around its own circle about the axle. At any instant the top of the rim moves one way and the bottom moves the opposite way, which is why the spinning wheel cannot be modeled as an object with a single velocity.

questions.q: The graph shows the angular position θ of a turntable as a function of time t. Which statement about the turntable's motion from t = 0 to t = 5 s is correct?
options: Its angular velocity has the same value at every instant.
Its angular velocity increases, since the graph keeps rising.
Its angular acceleration is positive, since the turntable keeps turning.
Its angular displacement is given by the area under the graph.
optionWhy: The angular velocity is the slope of the θ–t graph. The graph is a straight line, so its slope, 20 rad ÷ 5 s = 4 rad/s, is the same at every instant, and the angular acceleration is zero.

A student who reads the rising height of the graph as a rising angular velocity picks this. The height is the angular position, which does increase; the angular velocity is the slope, which stays the same.

A student who thinks a system needs an angular acceleration to keep rotating picks this. A turntable turning at a steady rate has zero angular acceleration; an angular acceleration is needed only to change the angular velocity.

A student who uses the area under every motion graph picks this. The area under an ω–t graph gives an angular displacement; on a θ–t graph the angular displacement is the change in height, here 20 rad − 0 = 20 rad.
questions.explain: The angular velocity is the slope of the θ–t graph. The graph is a straight line, so its slope, 20 rad ÷ 5 s = 4 rad/s, is the same at every instant, and the angular acceleration is zero.
questions.working: Slope = (20 − 0) rad ÷ (5 − 0) s = 4 rad/s, constant; α = 0. Δθ = 20 rad (change in height).

questions.q: A wheel rotates counterclockwise about a fixed axle with constant angular velocity ω. Point P is on the rim, a distance r from the axle. Which statement about P's velocity at any instant is correct?
options: It points toward the axle, the direction in which P accelerates.
It points away from the axle, since P tends to fly outward.
It stays the same at every instant, since P's speed rω is constant.
It is tangent to the rim, so its direction keeps changing.
optionWhy: A student who thinks velocity points the same way as acceleration picks this. P's acceleration does point toward the axle, but its velocity is along its path, tangent to the rim; the two are at right angles here.

A student who thinks points on a rotating object are thrown outward picks this. P stays on its circle; at each instant it moves along the tangent, and the rest of the wheel exerts forces on it that keep it on the circle.

A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity picks this. P's speed, rω, is constant, but velocity includes direction, and the direction of P's motion turns continuously as P goes around the axle, so the velocity changes.

P moves along a circle about the axle, so at any instant its velocity is along the tangent to that circle (in the counterclockwise sense of rotation), with magnitude v = rω. As P goes around, the tangent turns, so the velocity's direction changes continuously even though its magnitude stays rω.
questions.explain: P moves along a circle about the axle, so at any instant its velocity is along the tangent to that circle (in the counterclockwise sense of rotation), with magnitude v = rω. As P goes around, the tangent turns, so the velocity's direction changes continuously even though its magnitude stays rω.

questions.q: A wheel rotates counterclockwise about a fixed axle with constant angular velocity. Which statement about a point on the wheel's rim is correct?
options: Its tangential acceleration is zero, because α is zero.
Its acceleration is zero, as its speed is constant.
Its speed changes, since its direction of motion keeps changing.
Its acceleration points along its path, the way it moves.
optionWhy: With constant angular velocity, α = 0, so the tangential acceleration a_T = rα is zero and the point's speed does not change. The point still has a centripetal acceleration, v²/r, toward the axle, because the direction of its velocity changes.

A student who thinks an object moving at constant speed cannot be accelerating picks this. The point's speed is constant, but the direction of its velocity changes continuously, so it has a centripetal acceleration toward the axle.
A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity picks this. The DIRECTION of the velocity changes, but the speed, rω, stays constant because r and ω are constant.

A student who thinks acceleration points the same way as velocity picks this. At constant angular velocity the point's speed does not change, so it has no acceleration along its path; its only acceleration is centripetal, toward the axle, at right angles to its velocity.
questions.explain: With constant angular velocity, α = 0, so the tangential acceleration a_T = rα is zero and the point's speed does not change. The point still has a centripetal acceleration, v²/r, toward the axle, because the direction of its velocity changes.

questions.q: A light string is wrapped around a pulley of radius 0.0600 m that turns on a fixed axle. The string is pulled so that it unwinds without slipping while the pulley turns through 20.0 rad. What length of string unwinds from the pulley?
optionWhy: A student who uses the diameter, 0.120 m, in place of the radius picks this. The string leaves the rim, one radius (0.0600 m) from the axle, so Δs = rΔθ with r = 0.0600 m.
Each point on the rim travels an arc length Δs = rΔθ, and the string unwinds by that length: (0.0600 m)(20.0 rad) = 1.20 m. The equation applies directly because the angle is in radians.
A student who treats the 20.0 rad as 20.0 revolutions and multiplies by 2π picks this. The angle is already in radians, so Δs = rΔθ needs no conversion.
A student who converts 20.0 rad to degrees (about 1146°) before using Δs = rΔθ picks this. The equation holds only with the angle in radians; with degrees the result is 57.3 times too large.
questions.explain: Each point on the rim travels an arc length Δs = rΔθ, and the string unwinds by that length: (0.0600 m)(20.0 rad) = 1.20 m. The equation applies directly because the angle is in radians.
questions.working: Δs = rΔθ = (0.0600 m)(20.0 rad) = 1.20 m. Distractors: diameter 0.120 m → 2.40 m; ×2π → 7.54 m; degrees 1145.9° × 0.0600 m → 68.8 m.

questions.q: A door can rotate about its hinges. A student pushes on the door handle with a force directed along the surface of the door, straight toward the hinges. Which statement about the torque that this force exerts on the door about the hinges is correct?
options: It equals the force's magnitude times the handle's distance from the hinges.
It is zero, because the force has no component perpendicular to the door.
It equals the force's magnitude, because a torque is a turning force.
It is larger than it would be for the same push exerted nearer the hinges.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the whole force contributes, whatever its direction, multiplies the force by the distance. That product is the torque only for a force perpendicular to the door; a force directed along the door toward the hinges has no perpendicular component and exerts no torque.

Torque comes only from the component of a force perpendicular to the position vector from the axis to the point of application. This force points along the door, parallel to that position vector, so its perpendicular component is zero and so is the torque: the push presses the door against its hinges without turning it.

A student who treats torque as simply a turning force picks this. Torque and force are different quantities with different units (N·m and N), and a force directed along the line through the axis, as this one is, exerts no torque however large it is.

A student who thinks a force exerted farther from the axis always exerts a greater torque picks this. Distance matters only through the perpendicular component of the force; this push has none, so it exerts zero torque wherever along the door it is exerted.
questions.explain: Torque comes only from the component of a force perpendicular to the position vector from the axis to the point of application. This force points along the door, parallel to that position vector, so its perpendicular component is zero and so is the torque: the push presses the door against its hinges without turning it.

questions.q: A uniform rod is held horizontal by a hinge at its left end and a vertical string attached to its right end. A student is drawing a force diagram to analyze the torques exerted on the rod about the hinge. Which instruction for drawing the diagram is correct?
options: Draw every force on the rod from a single dot at the rod's center of mass.
Include the forces that the rod exerts on the hinge and on the string.
Leave out the hinge's force, since it exerts no torque about the hinge.
Start each force's arrow where that force is exerted on the rod.
optionWhy: A student who carries over the free-body diagram convention draws every force from the center of mass. That hides what is needed for torques: the string's force and the hinge's force are exerted at the ends of the rod, and their distances from the hinge matter.

A student who lists every force present at a contact picks this. The rod's push on the hinge and its pull on the string are exerted on the hinge and on the string, not on the rod; only forces exerted on the rod belong in its diagram.

A student who drops forces that exert no torque about the chosen axis picks this. The hinge's force does exert zero torque about the hinge, but it is still a force exerted on the rod, and a force diagram shows every force exerted on the system.

A force diagram, like a free-body diagram, shows each force exerted on the rod by another object, with its relative magnitude and direction. It also shows where each force is exerted: the weight at the rod's center, the string's force at the right end and the hinge's force at the left end, because those locations determine the torques.
questions.explain: A force diagram, like a free-body diagram, shows each force exerted on the rod by another object, with its relative magnitude and direction. It also shows where each force is exerted: the weight at the rod's center, the string's force at the right end and the hinge's force at the left end, because those locations determine the torques.

questions.q: The diagram shows a rigid bar pivoted at O and a horizontal force of 50 N exerted on the bar at its end P. What is the magnitude of the torque that this force exerts on the bar about O?
options: 30 N·m
40 N·m
50 N·m
70 N·m
optionWhy: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action of the force. The force is horizontal, so its line of action is the horizontal line through P, 0.60 m above O: τ = 50 N × 0.60 m = 30 N·m. The same result follows from τ = rF sin θ with r = 1.0 m and sin θ = 0.60.

A student who always uses the horizontal distance from the pivot, as in seesaw problems with vertical weights, gets 50 × 0.80 = 40 N·m. The lever arm must be perpendicular to the line of action; for a horizontal force that is the vertical distance, 0.60 m.

A student who takes the lever arm to be the distance from O to P, √(0.80² + 0.60²) = 1.0 m, gets 50 N·m. That would be right only if the force were perpendicular to the bar. The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from O to the force's line of action, 0.60 m.

A student who adds the horizontal and vertical distances, 0.80 m + 0.60 m = 1.4 m, gets 70 N·m. Perpendicular distances do not add as ordinary numbers, and only the distance perpendicular to the line of action, 0.60 m, is the lever arm.
questions.explain: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action of the force. The force is horizontal, so its line of action is the horizontal line through P, 0.60 m above O: τ = 50 N × 0.60 m = 30 N·m. The same result follows from τ = rF sin θ with r = 1.0 m and sin θ = 0.60.
questions.working: The line of action of the horizontal force is the horizontal line through P. The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from O to that line, which is the vertical distance, 0.60 m. τ = (50 N)(0.60 m) = 30 N·m. Check with τ = rF sin θ: r = √(0.80² + 0.60²) = 1.0 m, and the angle θ between the bar and the horizontal force has sin θ = 0.60/1.0 = 0.60, so τ = (1.0 m)(50 N)(0.60) = 30 N·m.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes what the rotational inertia of a rigid system about a given axis measures?
options: How fast the system is rotating about the axis at a given instant
The torque needed to keep the system rotating at a steady rate
How strongly the system resists a change in its rate of rotation
The total mass of the system, wherever that mass is located
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia measures how fast a system spins picks this. How fast it rotates is the angular velocity; rotational inertia measures how hard it is to change that angular velocity and does not depend on it.

A student who thinks rotation needs a continual torque to keep going picks this. Rotational inertia describes resistance to a change in rotation and is measured in kg·m², not N·m; a system has the same rotational inertia whether or not any torque is exerted on it.

Rotational inertia is the rotational counterpart of mass as a measure of inertia: the greater it is, the harder it is to start, stop, speed up or slow down the system's rotation about that axis. It depends on the system's mass and on how far that mass is from the axis.
A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass picks this. The distribution of the mass also matters: the same mass placed farther from the axis gives a greater rotational inertia.
questions.explain: Rotational inertia is the rotational counterpart of mass as a measure of inertia: the greater it is, the harder it is to start, stop, speed up or slow down the system's rotation about that axis. It depends on the system's mass and on how far that mass is from the axis.

questions.q: A bicycle wheel can rotate about its axle. Which change would increase the wheel's rotational inertia about the axle?
options: Moving some of its mass from the rim in toward the hub
Spinning the wheel at a faster rate about the same axle
Pushing on the rim, rather than near the hub, to turn it
Moving some of its mass from the hub out to the rim
optionWhy: A student who thinks mass far from the axis is easier to turn, because of leverage, picks this. Leverage applies to where a force is exerted, not to where mass is; moving mass toward the hub reduces the rotational inertia.

A student who thinks rotational inertia measures how fast the wheel spins picks this. Spinning faster increases the wheel's angular velocity; its rotational inertia depends only on its mass and how that mass is placed, so it does not change.

A student who thinks rotational inertia depends on how the wheel is pushed picks this. Where the push is exerted changes the torque, not the rotational inertia, which is set by the wheel's mass and its distribution about the axle.

Rotational inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. Moving mass from the hub to the rim puts it farther from the axle, so each piece moved contributes more (mr² for each piece) and the total increases.
questions.explain: Rotational inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. Moving mass from the hub to the rim puts it farther from the axle, so each piece moved contributes more (mr² for each piece) and the total increases.

questions.q: A small object of mass m is fastened to a light rod a distance r from the rod's axis of rotation. It is replaced by a small object of mass m/3 fastened a distance 3r from the same axis. The new rotational inertia of the system about the axis is how many times the original rotational inertia?
options: ×⅓
optionWhy: A student who takes I to be proportional to r, not r², gets ⅓ × 3 = 1. The distance is squared: tripling it multiplies I by 9, so the overall factor is ⅓ × 9 = 3.
I = mr². Dividing the mass by 3 multiplies I by ⅓, and tripling the distance multiplies it by 3² = 9, so the new rotational inertia is ⅓ × 9 = 3 times the original.
A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass gets a factor of ⅓ from the smaller mass. Moving the object three times as far out multiplies I by 9, which outweighs the smaller mass.
A student who attends only to the distance gets a factor of 3² = 9. The mass has also been divided by 3, so the factor is 9 × ⅓ = 3.
questions.explain: I = mr². Dividing the mass by 3 multiplies I by ⅓, and tripling the distance multiplies it by 3² = 9, so the new rotational inertia is ⅓ × 9 = 3 times the original.
questions.working: Original: I = mr². New: I′ = (m/3)(3r)² = (m/3)(9r²) = 3mr². I′/I = 3.

questions.q: An electric fan is switched on, and after a few seconds its blades turn at a constant angular velocity. Which statement about the torques exerted on the blades while they turn at this constant angular velocity is correct?
options: The motor's torque is balanced by the opposing torques.
The motor's torque exceeds the torques that oppose the rotation.
The net torque is not zero, since each point on a blade accelerates.
No torques are exerted, since the blades are in equilibrium.
optionWhy: A constant angular velocity means rotational equilibrium, so the net torque on the blades is zero. Torques are still exerted on them: the motor's torque in the sense of rotation, and the opposing torques of air resistance and axle friction, which have the same total magnitude.

A student who thinks steady rotation needs a net torque in its direction picks this. If the motor's torque were larger, the net torque would not be zero and the blades would speed up. The motor's torque only has to balance the opposing torques.

A student who treats the acceleration of points on the blades as a change in rotation picks this. Each point has a centripetal acceleration because its direction of motion changes, but the blades' angular velocity is constant, and rotational equilibrium needs only a zero net torque.

A student who thinks equilibrium means no torques are exerted picks this. The motor exerts a torque, and air resistance and friction exert opposing torques; they balance, so the net torque is zero, but none of them is zero.
questions.explain: A constant angular velocity means rotational equilibrium, so the net torque on the blades is zero. Torques are still exerted on them: the motor's torque in the sense of rotation, and the opposing torques of air resistance and axle friction, which have the same total magnitude.

questions.q: Two identical uniform rods, X and Y, lie at rest on a horizontal surface with negligible friction. Two horizontal forces, each of magnitude F and perpendicular to the rod, are then exerted on each rod, one at each end, and they stay perpendicular to the rod. On rod X the two forces point in the same direction; on rod Y they point in opposite directions. Which rod or rods remain in rotational equilibrium while the forces are exerted?
options: Only rod Y, since the two forces on it add up to zero
Only rod X, as its torques about the center cancel
Both rods, as each of the rods starts from rest
Neither rod, as forces exert torques on both of them
optionWhy: A student who thinks that forces adding to zero guarantee rotational equilibrium picks this. The forces on rod Y do cancel, so its center of mass stays at rest, but they act along different lines and both turn the rod the same way: the net torque on Y is FL, not zero, so Y starts to rotate.

On rod X the forces act at equal distances on either side of the center and point the same way, so about the center one exerts a clockwise torque and the other an equal counterclockwise torque: the net torque is zero and X's angular velocity stays zero, even though its center of mass speeds up. On rod Y the forces add to zero but both turn the rod the same way, so Y starts to rotate. Rotational and translational equilibrium are independent.

A student who takes 'at rest' to mean 'in equilibrium' picks this. Both rods start with zero angular velocity, but rotational equilibrium means the angular velocity stays constant. The net torque on rod Y is not zero, so its angular velocity changes as soon as the forces are exerted.

A student who thinks equilibrium means that no torques are exerted picks this. Torques are exerted on both rods, but on rod X they are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense, so the net torque is zero and X does not start to rotate. Equilibrium needs a zero net torque, not the absence of torques.
questions.explain: On rod X the forces act at equal distances on either side of the center and point the same way, so about the center one exerts a clockwise torque and the other an equal counterclockwise torque: the net torque is zero and X's angular velocity stays zero, even though its center of mass speeds up. On rod Y the forces add to zero but both turn the rod the same way, so Y starts to rotate. Rotational and translational equilibrium are independent.

questions.q: A uniform horizontal rod of weight 40 N is attached to a wall by a hinge at its left end. A sign of weight 16 N hangs from the rod's right end, and a cable attached to the rod's right end holds the rod at rest, as shown in the diagram. Use sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80. What is the tension in the cable?
optionWhy: Taking torques about the hinge removes the unknown hinge force. Only the component of the tension perpendicular to the rod, T sin 37°, has a torque about the hinge, with lever arm L. Balancing it against the rod's weight (at L/2) and the sign (at L): 0.60T × L = 40 N × L/2 + 16 N × L = 36 N × L, so T = 60 N.
A student who puts the rod's whole weight at its far end picks this: 0.60T = 40 N + 16 N gives 93 N. A uniform rod's weight acts at its center, so its lever arm about the hinge is L/2, not L.

A student who treats the whole tension as perpendicular to the rod picks this: T × L = 36 N × L gives 36 N. Only the perpendicular component, T sin 37°, has a torque about the hinge; the component along the rod points through the hinge.

A student who takes the perpendicular component as T cos 37° picks this: 0.80T = 36 N gives 45 N. The diagram shows that the 37° angle is between the cable and the rod, so T cos 37° is the component along the rod and the perpendicular component is T sin 37° = 0.60T.
questions.explain: Taking torques about the hinge removes the unknown hinge force. Only the component of the tension perpendicular to the rod, T sin 37°, has a torque about the hinge, with lever arm L. Balancing it against the rod's weight (at L/2) and the sign (at L): 0.60T × L = 40 N × L/2 + 16 N × L = 36 N × L, so T = 60 N.
questions.working: Take torques about the hinge, so the unknown hinge force has zero lever arm. Let the rod's length be L. Counterclockwise: the cable's perpendicular component T sin 37° = 0.60T at lever arm L. Clockwise: the rod's weight 40 N at its center (lever arm L/2) and the sign's weight 16 N at the end (lever arm L). Zero net torque: 0.60T × L = 40 N × L/2 + 16 N × L = 36 N × L, so T = 36 N ÷ 0.60 = 60 N.

questions.q: A rigid wheel turns on a fixed axle. The net torque exerted on the wheel is not zero. Which statement about the wheel must be true?
options: Its angular velocity is changing with time.
It turns in the same sense as the net torque.
Its angular speed is increasing with time.
It turns at a steady rate set by the torque.
optionWhy: A nonzero net torque means the torques on the wheel are unbalanced, so its angular velocity changes: it may speed up, slow down or reverse. Only the change is certain; the sense of rotation, and whether the wheel speeds up or slows down, depend on how the net torque compares with the rotation.

A student who thinks a wheel turns in the sense of the net torque picks this. The net torque sets the sense of the CHANGE in angular velocity: a wheel turning counterclockwise with a clockwise net torque on it keeps turning counterclockwise for a while as it slows down.
A student who thinks a net torque always speeds a rotation up picks this. If the net torque is opposite to the rotation, as when friction or a brake acts on the wheel, the angular speed decreases.
A student who thinks a torque produces a steady rotation picks this. A steady rate of rotation needs a zero net torque; a nonzero net torque makes the angular velocity change.
questions.explain: A nonzero net torque means the torques on the wheel are unbalanced, so its angular velocity changes: it may speed up, slow down or reverse. Only the change is certain; the sense of rotation, and whether the wheel speeds up or slows down, depend on how the net torque compares with the rotation.

questions.q: A solid disk of radius 0.50 m and rotational inertia 0.25 kg·m² turns on a fixed axle. A string wrapped around its rim is pulled with a constant force of 2.0 N, tangent to the rim, in the sense in which the disk is turning. Friction at the axle exerts a constant torque of 0.25 N·m that opposes the rotation. What is the magnitude of the disk's angular acceleration?
options: 4.0 rad/s²
5.0 rad/s²
8.0 rad/s²
3.0 rad/s²
optionWhy: A student who uses the pull's torque as the net torque picks this: 1.0 N·m ÷ 0.25 kg·m² = 4.0 rad/s². Newton's second law in rotational form uses the NET torque, so the frictional torque must be subtracted first.
A student who adds the two torques, 1.0 N·m + 0.25 N·m, picks this. Friction opposes the rotation, so its torque has the opposite sign: the net torque is 1.0 N·m − 0.25 N·m = 0.75 N·m.

A student who divides the force by the rotational inertia, 2.0 N ÷ 0.25 kg·m², picks this. Angular acceleration depends on torque, not force: the pull's torque is rF = 1.0 N·m, and the net torque is 0.75 N·m. (F/I does not even have the units of rad/s².)

The pull exerts a torque rF = (0.50 m)(2.0 N) = 1.0 N·m in the sense of rotation, and friction exerts 0.25 N·m in the opposite sense, so τ_net = 0.75 N·m. Then α = τ_net/I = 0.75 N·m ÷ 0.25 kg·m² = 3.0 rad/s².
questions.explain: The pull exerts a torque rF = (0.50 m)(2.0 N) = 1.0 N·m in the sense of rotation, and friction exerts 0.25 N·m in the opposite sense, so τ_net = 0.75 N·m. Then α = τ_net/I = 0.75 N·m ÷ 0.25 kg·m² = 3.0 rad/s².
questions.working: Torque of the pull: τ = rF = (0.50 m)(2.0 N) = 1.0 N·m, in the sense of rotation. Frictional torque: 0.25 N·m, opposite. τ_net = 1.0 N·m − 0.25 N·m = 0.75 N·m. α = τ_net/I = 0.75 N·m ÷ 0.25 kg·m² = 3.0 rad/s².

questions.q: A light rod can rotate in a horizontal plane about a vertical axle through its center, with negligible friction. Two small spheres, each of mass m, are fixed to the rod, one on each side of the axle at distance r from it. A constant force F exerted perpendicular to the rod at distance d from the axle gives the rod an angular acceleration α₀. The spheres are then moved to distance 2r from the axle, and the same force F is exerted at distance 2d. The new angular acceleration is how many times α₀?
options: ½
¼
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass picks this: the torque doubles and I is taken as unchanged. Moving the same mass farther from the axle increases I, here by a factor of 4, since I = mr².

Doubling the lever arm doubles the torque: τ = F(2d) = 2Fd. Doubling the spheres' distance multiplies the rotational inertia by 2² = 4: I = 2m(2r)² = 4 × 2mr². So α = τ_net/I changes by a factor of 2/4 = ½.
A student who takes rotational inertia to be proportional to r instead of r² picks this: the torque doubles and I is taken to double, so α seems unchanged. With I = mr², doubling r multiplies I by 4.

A student who treats the same force as giving the same torque picks this: I is correctly multiplied by 4, but the torque is taken as unchanged. Exerting the same force at twice the distance doubles the torque.
questions.explain: Doubling the lever arm doubles the torque: τ = F(2d) = 2Fd. Doubling the spheres' distance multiplies the rotational inertia by 2² = 4: I = 2m(2r)² = 4 × 2mr². So α = τ_net/I changes by a factor of 2/4 = ½.
questions.working: Originally τ = Fd and I = 2mr², so α₀ = Fd/(2mr²). Afterwards τ = F(2d) = 2Fd and I = 2m(2r)² = 8mr² = 4 × 2mr². α = 2Fd/(8mr²) = (2/4) × Fd/(2mr²) = ½α₀.

questions.q: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disk have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its plane, with the same angular speed ω. How does the angular momentum of the hoop about its axis compare with that of the disk about its axis?
options: They are equal, since the masses and angular speeds are equal.
The hoop's is greater, since its mass is all at the rim.
The disk's is greater, since the disk is solid all the way through.
Both are zero, since neither object's center is moving.
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass picks this. Rotational inertia also depends on how the mass is distributed: the hoop's mass is farther from the axis, so at the same ω the hoop has more angular momentum.

L = Iω and the angular speeds are equal, so the comparison is decided by rotational inertia. All of the hoop's mass is a distance R from the axis, while much of the disk's mass is closer to it, so the hoop has the greater I and the greater angular momentum.

A student who thinks a solid object is harder to turn than a hollow one of the same mass picks this. The masses are equal; what matters is where the mass is. The disk's mass is on average closer to the axis, so its rotational inertia, and its angular momentum at the same ω, is smaller.

A student who thinks an object spinning in place has no angular momentum picks this. Each object's LINEAR momentum is zero because its center of mass is at rest, but each has angular momentum L = Iω about its axis because it is spinning.
questions.explain: L = Iω and the angular speeds are equal, so the comparison is decided by rotational inertia. All of the hoop's mass is a distance R from the axis, while much of the disk's mass is closer to it, so the hoop has the greater I and the greater angular momentum.

questions.q: During a certain time interval, the net angular impulse delivered to a spinning wheel is zero. Which statement about the wheel must be true?
options: Its angular momentum is the same at the end as at the start.
Its angular momentum at the end of the interval is zero.
No torque was exerted on the wheel at any time in the interval.
Its angular speed fell, as no net angular impulse kept it going.
optionWhy: The change in angular momentum equals the net angular impulse. A net angular impulse of zero means ΔL = 0, so the wheel ends the interval with the same angular momentum it began with, whatever torques acted along the way.

A student who takes the angular impulse to be the final angular momentum picks this. Zero net angular impulse means zero CHANGE: a wheel that was spinning is still spinning at the end with the same angular momentum.
A student who reads 'zero net' as 'nothing acted' picks this. Torques in opposite senses can act, together or one after another, and their angular impulses can add to zero; only the total is zero.

A student who thinks a spinning object needs a net torque to keep turning picks this. With zero net angular impulse the angular momentum does not change, so a rigid wheel keeps the same angular speed.
questions.explain: The change in angular momentum equals the net angular impulse. A net angular impulse of zero means ΔL = 0, so the wheel ends the interval with the same angular momentum it began with, whatever torques acted along the way.
